title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
syllabus: Introduce Artificial Intelligence (AI), explain the basic idea of machines performing tasks that normally require human intelligence, and establish a simple mental model of AI for complete beginners.
objectives: Understand the meaning of Artificial Intelligence
Understand why AI is called intelligence
Distinguish AI from ordinary software at a basic level
Recognize simple examples of AI in daily life

title: AI in Everyday Life
syllabus: Show how AI already appears in everyday activities such as search, recommendations, maps, smartphones, cameras, banking, shopping, entertainment, translation and customer service.
objectives: Recognize AI applications in daily life
Understand that AI is broader than chatbots
Connect familiar products and services with AI concepts
Identify AI examples in the learner's own environment

title: Computers, Software and AI: What Is the Difference?
syllabus: Explain the relationship and differences between hardware, software, traditional programs, automation and AI systems using simple real-world examples.
objectives: Understand how traditional programs follow explicit instructions
Understand at a basic level how AI systems differ from rule-based software

title: Why Was Artificial Intelligence Created?
syllabus: Explain the goals and historical motivation behind AI, including the desire to make machines solve problems, recognize patterns, understand language, assist people and automate complex tasks.
objectives: Learn the basic historical motivation for AI
Understand major categories of problems AI attempts to solve
Avoid the misconception that AI appeared suddenly with modern chatbots

title: Can Machines Really Think?
syllabus: Explore the meaning of thinking, intelligence, reasoning, learning and understanding in machines. Introduce the difference between human intelligence and machine capabilities without claiming that current AI is human-like in every way.
objectives: Distinguish human thinking from machine computation
Understand that AI can perform intelligent-looking tasks without being human
Introduce the idea of machine reasoning and limitations

title: What Is Data?
syllabus: Introduce data as information that AI systems can use, including text, numbers, images, audio, video and sensor information. Explain why data is fundamental to modern AI.
objectives: Understand why AI systems need data
Connect everyday information with AI data

title: What Is an AI Model?
syllabus: Explain what an AI model is, how a model represents patterns learned from data, and how models are used to produce predictions, classifications or generated outputs.
objectives: Understand the meaning of an AI model
Understand the relationship between data and models
Distinguish a model from an AI application
Understand that different models can perform different tasks

title: Training vs Inference
syllabus: Introduce the two fundamental stages of modern AI systems: training, where a model learns patterns from data, and inference, where a trained model processes new input to produce an output.
objectives: Understand the difference between learning and using a trained model
Follow a simple end-to-end AI model lifecycle

title: AI vs Machine Learning vs Deep Learning vs Generative AI
syllabus: Clearly explain the relationship between Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, Deep Learning and Generative AI, including what each term means and how they relate to one another.
objectives: Understand the relationship among the four concepts

title: Prediction, Classification and Generation
syllabus: Introduce three fundamental types of AI outputs: prediction of values, classification into categories, and generation of new content. Use simple examples suitable for children and adults.
objectives: Recognize these task types in real AI applications

title: Supervised, Unsupervised and Reinforcement Learning
syllabus: Introduce the three major learning approaches in Machine Learning: supervised learning using labeled examples, unsupervised learning for discovering patterns without labels, and reinforcement learning through actions, feedback and rewards.
objectives: Compare the three approaches using simple real-world examples
Recognize when each learning approach is useful

title: Dataset, Data Points, Features and Labels
syllabus: Explain the basic structure of machine learning data: datasets, individual data points or records, rows, columns, features, labels and targets. Show how input features are connected to the answer a model learns to predict.
objectives: Understand a data point or record

title: Training Data, Validation Data and Test Data
syllabus: Explain why machine learning datasets are separated for learning, model development and final evaluation. Introduce training data, validation data, test data, generalization, overfitting and the basic idea of data leakage.
objectives: Understand why unseen data is important
Understand generalization at a basic level
Recognize the basic problem of data leakage

title: How Does a Machine Learning Model Learn?
syllabus: Explain the basic learning loop of a machine learning model: receiving inputs, producing predictions, comparing predictions with known answers, measuring error and adjusting model parameters to improve future predictions.
objectives: Understand the basic ML learning loop
Understand parameters at an intuitive level
Understand how repeated training improves a model

title: What Is a Neural Network?
syllabus: Introduce neural networks using a simple intuitive explanation of artificial neurons, layers, connections, weights and information flow. Connect neural networks to the broader idea of learning patterns from data.
objectives: Understand what a neural network is
Understand connections and weights at a basic level
Understand why neural networks are useful for complex patterns

title: What Is Deep Learning?
syllabus: Explain Deep Learning as a branch of Machine Learning that uses neural networks with multiple layers. Show why deeper networks can learn complex representations and introduce common applications without going deeply into mathematics yet.
objectives: Understand the relationship between ML and Deep Learning
Understand why multiple neural-network layers matter
Prepare for later technical study of neural networks

title: What Is Natural Language Processing?
syllabus: Introduce Natural Language Processing (NLP), the field concerned with enabling computers to process and work with human language. Cover text understanding, translation, summarization, classification, question answering and generation at a high level.
objectives: Understand why human language is difficult for computers
Connect NLP with modern AI assistants and language models

title: What Is Computer Vision?
syllabus: Introduce Computer Vision, the field of AI that enables machines to analyze images and video. Explain image classification, object detection, recognition and visual understanding using accessible examples.
objectives: Understand how AI works with images and video

title: What Is Speech AI?
syllabus: Introduce AI systems that process human speech and audio, including speech recognition, text-to-speech, speaker understanding and audio analysis. Explain how speech AI connects human voice with machine systems.

title: What Is Generative AI?
syllabus: Introduce Generative AI as AI that can create new content such as text, images, audio, video and code. Explain the difference between generating content and simply classifying or predicting existing information.
objectives: Understand how generation differs from classification and prediction
Recognize major types of generated content
Understand why Generative AI became a major AI technology
Connect Generative AI with later study of foundation models and LLMs

title: What Is a Language Model?
syllabus: Introduce language models as AI systems trained to work with language and predict or generate sequences of tokens. Explain the basic idea using simple examples before introducing technical details.
objectives: Understand what a language model is
Understand that language models work with sequences of text
Understand the basic idea of next-token prediction
Recognize language models in modern AI applications
Prepare for later study of Large Language Models

title: What Is a Foundation Model?
syllabus: Explain foundation models as broadly trained AI models that can serve as a base for many downstream tasks and applications. Introduce the idea of adapting or using one model for multiple purposes.
objectives: Understand the meaning of foundation model
Understand how one model can support many tasks
Distinguish foundation models from individual AI applications
Recognize examples across language, vision and multimodal AI

title: What Is Multimodal AI?
syllabus: Introduce Multimodal AI systems that can work with more than one type of information, such as text, images, audio and video. Explain why combining modalities can make AI applications more capable.
objectives: Understand audio and video as AI inputs or outputs

title: What Is an AI Agent?
syllabus: Introduce AI agents as systems that can use models, tools, memory and actions to pursue goals. Clearly distinguish an agent from a simple chatbot and explain the concept without going deeply into implementation.
objectives: Understand the basic meaning of AI agent
Understand the difference between an agent and a chatbot
Understand the idea of an agent loop
Prepare for the advanced Agent phase later in the curriculum

title: AI Models vs AI Tools vs AI Applications
syllabus: Teach the difference between an underlying AI model, an AI-powered tool and a complete AI application or product. Explain how models become useful to people through interfaces, workflows, data and tools.
objectives: Understand what an AI model is
Understand what an AI tool is
Understand what an AI application is
Avoid confusing an AI model with the complete application built around it

title: How Does an AI Application Work?
syllabus: Explain the basic architecture of an AI application from user input through application logic, model or API processing, optional tools or databases, and final output. Build an intuitive foundation for later AI engineering.
objectives: Understand the basic flow of an AI application
Understand user input and AI output
Understand the role of application logic
Understand that AI applications may use databases, tools and APIs
Prepare for later AI engineering concepts

title: Humans and AI: Who Does What?
syllabus: Explore how humans and AI systems can work together. Explain strengths and limitations of both, emphasizing human judgment, creativity, responsibility, context and AI's ability to process patterns and information at scale.
objectives: Understand complementary strengths of humans and AI
Understand why human judgment remains important
Identify tasks where AI can assist people
Understand human responsibility when using AI
Introduce the concept of human-in-the-loop systems

title: What AI Can and Cannot Do
syllabus: Build a realistic understanding of AI capabilities and limitations. Cover pattern recognition, generation, reasoning, uncertainty, hallucinations, lack of guaranteed truth and dependence on data, tools and system design.
objectives: Understand why AI can produce incorrect information
Understand why confident output does not guarantee truth

title: AI Myths, Mistakes and Misunderstandings
syllabus: Correct common misconceptions about AI, including the ideas that AI is always correct, always intelligent in a human sense, completely autonomous, conscious, unbiased or capable of replacing every human task.
objectives: Distinguish AI capability from science fiction
Understand why AI outputs require appropriate verification
Develop critical thinking about AI claims

title: AI Foundations Review and Challenge
syllabus: Review the complete first 29 days of AI foundations without simply repeating the lessons. Connect the major concepts into one coherent mental model and use questions, scenarios and a mini challenge to test understanding.
objectives: Connect the major AI foundation concepts
Distinguish AI, ML, Deep Learning and Generative AI
Understand data, models, training and inference
Recognize language, vision, speech, multimodal and agent systems
Identify personal knowledge gaps before moving to AI literacy and prompting

title: How to Talk to AI Effectively
syllabus: Introduce effective communication with AI systems. Explain that useful AI output depends heavily on the quality, clarity and completeness of the user's instructions.
objectives: Understand the basic concept of prompting
Understand why vague instructions produce inconsistent results
Learn to state a clear goal
Understand that prompting is a communication skill

title: What Is a Prompt?
syllabus: Explain what a prompt is and introduce the basic components of a useful prompt: task, context, requirements and desired output. Use simple examples for children, students, workers and professionals.
objectives: Identify the task in a prompt

title: Clear Instructions and Specific Requests
syllabus: Teach how to make AI instructions precise, unambiguous and actionable. Compare vague prompts with specific prompts and show how constraints improve usefulness.

title: Giving Context to AI
syllabus: Explain why relevant context helps an AI system produce more useful responses. Teach users how to provide background, audience, situation, goals and important constraints without unnecessary information.
objectives: Separate useful context from irrelevant information

title: Giving AI a Role and Perspective
syllabus: Explain how asking an AI to respond from a particular professional or audience perspective can help structure an answer. Teach role prompting responsibly without implying that a role guarantees expertise or correctness.
objectives: Understand the limits of role prompting
Avoid treating a role instruction as proof of expertise

title: Controlling AI Output Format
syllabus: Teach users to specify how they want AI output presented, including lists, tables, headings, summaries, JSON, step-by-step instructions and other structured formats.
objectives: Understand why output constraints are useful
Introduce machine-readable formats such as JSON at a basic level

title: Few-Shot Prompting: Teaching by Examples
syllabus: Introduce the idea of showing an AI model examples of the desired input-output pattern before asking it to perform a similar task. Explain zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting intuitively.

title: Breaking a Large Task into Smaller Tasks
syllabus: Teach task decomposition: dividing a complex request into smaller logical steps that AI can handle more reliably. Introduce workflows and staged prompting.
objectives: Break complex goals into smaller steps
Understand why one giant prompt is not always best

title: Asking AI to Improve Its Own Output
syllabus: Introduce iterative prompting: reviewing an initial AI response, identifying weaknesses and asking for targeted improvements. Teach critique-and-revise workflows without assuming the AI's self-evaluation is always correct.
objectives: Understand that AI self-critique can also contain mistakes

title: The Complete Beginner Prompt Framework
syllabus: Combine the prompting foundations into a reusable framework containing goal, context, role or perspective when useful, inputs, constraints, process requirements and output format. Apply the framework to practical tasks from education, business, personal productivity and creativity.
objectives: Combine the major beginner prompting techniques
Apply prompting to multiple real-world situations
Build a reusable personal prompt template

title: AI for Learning and Education
syllabus: Teach how AI can support learning as a tutor, explainer, practice partner, quiz creator and study assistant while emphasizing that learners should understand concepts rather than blindly copy AI answers.
objectives: Use AI as a learning assistant
Ask AI to explain concepts at different difficulty levels
Use AI for revision and feedback
Understand the difference between learning with AI and copying from AI

title: AI for Research and Information Discovery
syllabus: Explain how AI can help discover, organize, compare and summarize information. Teach the difference between generating an answer and conducting reliable research, including the need to verify important claims against trustworthy sources.
objectives: Distinguish AI-generated claims from verified evidence

title: AI for Writing and Communication
syllabus: Teach practical AI-assisted writing for messages, emails, articles, reports, applications, presentations and social content while emphasizing human review, authenticity and appropriate tone.
objectives: Use AI to draft written content

title: AI for Translation and Multilingual Communication
syllabus: Explain how AI can translate and transform content between languages and styles. Cover useful applications, limitations, cultural context, terminology and the importance of human verification for sensitive or high-stakes translations.
objectives: Translate while preserving meaning and tone
Know when human review is necessary

title: AI for Summarization and Information Compression
syllabus: Teach AI-assisted summarization of long text, meetings, articles, reports and notes. Explain different summary styles such as executive summaries, bullet summaries and action-item summaries.
objectives: Understand the risk of missing important context

title: AI for Brainstorming and Creativity
syllabus: Show how AI can generate ideas, alternatives, outlines, names, stories, designs and creative directions. Teach users to treat AI as a creative collaborator rather than an unquestionable source of originality or quality.
objectives: Combine human creativity with AI assistance

title: AI for Personal Productivity
syllabus: Teach practical AI uses for planning, prioritization, checklists, note organization, routine tasks, decision preparation and personal workflows while keeping final decisions with the user.
objectives: Use AI to improve personal workflows

title: AI for Business and Office Work
syllabus: Introduce practical AI applications in business and office environments including document drafting, meeting summaries, customer communication, analysis, reporting, presentations and workflow assistance.
objectives: Use AI for routine office work

title: AI for Small Businesses and Entrepreneurs
syllabus: Show how small businesses and entrepreneurs can use AI for market research, customer support, content creation, planning, product ideas, documentation, basic analysis and automation while emphasizing validation and responsible use.
objectives: Identify AI opportunities in small businesses
Use AI for business idea development
Use AI for documentation and planning
Evaluate whether an AI use case creates real business value

title: AI Productivity Challenge: Solve a Real Problem
syllabus: Bring together the first 20 days of practical AI literacy and prompting through a real-world challenge. The learner chooses an education, personal, business or creative problem and designs a complete AI-assisted workflow.
objectives: Apply prompting skills to a real problem
Evaluate the usefulness of the result
Identify risks and required human verification

title: Prompt Engineering: From Simple Prompts to Reliable Instructions
syllabus: Introduce Prompt Engineering as the systematic design, testing and refinement of instructions for AI systems. Move beyond basic prompting toward repeatable and reliable task instructions.
objectives: Distinguish casual prompting from systematic prompt design
Identify the components of a reliable prompt
Understand the importance of testing prompts
Create reusable prompts for recurring tasks

title: Prompt Roles, Goals, Context and Constraints
syllabus: Develop a structured prompt framework using role or perspective when useful, clearly defined goals, relevant context, constraints, inputs and expected outputs. Explain when each component helps and when unnecessary instructions should be avoided.

title: Few-Shot Prompting for Consistent Results
syllabus: Go deeper into example-based prompting. Teach how carefully selected examples can communicate desired patterns, formatting and classification behavior, and explain how poor examples can create poor results.

title: Structured Output and JSON Prompting
syllabus: Teach how to request predictable structured outputs such as JSON, tables, lists and predefined fields. Explain why structured outputs are important when AI responses will be consumed by software.
objectives: Understand the difference between natural-language output and structured output

title: Prompt Chaining and Multi-Step AI Workflows
syllabus: Teach how a complex AI task can be divided into multiple connected prompts or stages. Explain how outputs from one stage can become inputs to another and how staged workflows can improve control.
objectives: Identify when chaining is better than one large prompt

title: Context Management and Long Conversations
syllabus: Explain how AI systems use conversation context and why long interactions can become difficult to manage. Teach users to organize important information, restate critical requirements and maintain a clean working context.
objectives: Understand context limits at a conceptual level
Separate permanent requirements from temporary instructions

title: Reasoning-Oriented Task Design
syllabus: Teach how to structure difficult tasks so an AI system can analyze requirements, identify assumptions, compare alternatives and produce a checked result. Focus on observable reasoning steps and useful intermediate artifacts rather than requiring hidden chain-of-thought.
objectives: Break difficult problems into logical stages
Use intermediate checks and structured reasoning outputs
Understand that apparent reasoning can still contain errors

title: Self-Checking, Critique and Verification Prompts
syllabus: Teach practical methods for asking AI to inspect its own output for missing requirements, contradictions, formatting errors and unsupported claims. Emphasize that AI self-checking is an additional safeguard, not a guarantee of correctness.
objectives: Ask for alternative answers or critiques
Understand the limits of AI self-verification

title: Prompt Evaluation and Testing
syllabus: Introduce systematic prompt evaluation using test cases, expected behavior, consistency, accuracy, completeness and failure analysis. Explain why a prompt that works once is not necessarily a reliable prompt.
objectives: Improve prompts based on evidence rather than intuition

title: Prompt Engineering Project
syllabus: Combine the advanced prompting concepts into a practical project. Design, test and refine a reusable AI workflow for a real task, including structured instructions, examples, constraints, output format, validation and failure handling.
objectives: Test the workflow with multiple cases

title: Understanding AI Model Families
syllabus: Introduce the idea that AI is not one model or one technology. Explain model families and specialized models for language, vision, speech, generation, reasoning and other tasks.
objectives: Understand the idea of AI model families
Understand why different models may be needed for different problems

title: Small Models vs Large Models
syllabus: Explain the practical differences between smaller and larger AI models, including capability, latency, resource requirements, cost and suitability for different tasks. Emphasize that larger does not automatically mean better for every use case.
objectives: Understand small and large AI models
Choose model size based on task requirements
Avoid assuming that the largest model is always the best

title: Open Models vs Proprietary Models
syllabus: Explain the difference between openly available model weights or open-source/open-weight ecosystems and proprietary hosted models. Cover practical considerations such as control, licensing, customization, infrastructure and access.
objectives: Understand open and open-weight model concepts
Recognize that 'open' can mean different things in AI

title: Cloud AI vs Local AI
syllabus: Compare AI models accessed through cloud services with models running locally on personal or organizational hardware. Explain privacy, cost, performance, hardware requirements, connectivity and operational trade-offs.
objectives: Choose an appropriate deployment approach for simple scenarios

title: Model Quality, Speed and Cost Trade-offs
syllabus: Teach the three-way practical trade-off among quality, latency and cost when selecting AI models. Explain why the best model for a production application depends on requirements rather than benchmark scores alone.
objectives: Select models according to real-world requirements

title: Context Length and Long-Context AI
syllabus: Explain context windows and the amount of information an AI model can process within a particular interaction. Introduce tokens conceptually and explain why context capacity matters for documents, conversations and large workflows.
objectives: Understand tokens at a basic level
Recognize challenges of very long context
Choose context strategies for large inputs

title: Multimodal Models and Model Capabilities
syllabus: Explain how modern models may support multiple modalities such as text, image, audio and video. Teach learners to evaluate which inputs and outputs a model actually supports instead of assuming all AI models have the same capabilities.
objectives: Match model capabilities to application requirements
Verify actual model capabilities before designing a workflow

title: AI Model Benchmarks and Leaderboards
syllabus: Introduce AI benchmarks as standardized evaluations used to compare models. Explain what benchmarks can reveal and what they cannot, including differences between benchmark performance and real-world usefulness.
objectives: Avoid choosing models based on one score alone

title: Choosing the Right AI Model for a Task
syllabus: Teach a practical model-selection framework based on task type, accuracy requirements, latency, cost, privacy, context size, modalities, deployment environment and reliability requirements.
objectives: Select an appropriate model for a practical scenario

title: AI Model Selection Challenge
syllabus: Apply the previous model-selection concepts to multiple realistic scenarios such as education, customer support, document processing, image analysis, coding and personal assistants. Require learners to justify model choices using measurable requirements.

title: What Is Machine Learning?
syllabus: Move from general AI concepts into the technical foundations of Machine Learning. Explain Machine Learning as a way of building systems that learn useful patterns from data instead of relying only on explicitly written rules.
objectives: Explain how ML relates to AI
Compare rule-based programming with learning from data

title: Features, Labels and Targets in Machine Learning
syllabus: Deepen the learner's understanding of features, labels and targets and show how they are represented in real machine learning problems for classification and regression.
objectives: Convert real-world problems into ML inputs and targets
Distinguish classification targets from numerical targets

title: Classification: Predicting Categories
syllabus: Teach classification as a Machine Learning task where a model predicts one or more categories. Introduce binary and multiclass classification using practical examples such as spam detection, disease screening and image recognition.
objectives: Understand predicted classes and probabilities at a basic level

title: Regression: Predicting Numerical Values
syllabus: Teach regression as a Machine Learning task for predicting numerical values. Use examples such as house prices, sales, demand and temperature while distinguishing regression from classification.

title: Linear Regression: The First Predictive Model
syllabus: Introduce linear regression as a simple mathematical model that relates input features to a numerical target. Explain the idea of a line, coefficients, intercept and prediction intuitively before progressing toward mathematical formulation.
objectives: Understand the idea of linear regression
Use a simple linear relationship for prediction

title: Classification with Logistic Regression
syllabus: Introduce logistic regression as a simple classification algorithm. Explain probability-based classification and decision boundaries intuitively, while preparing learners for more mathematical treatment later.
objectives: Compare logistic regression with linear regression

title: Decision Trees and Rule-Based Learning
syllabus: Explain decision trees as models that make predictions through a sequence of learned decisions. Show nodes, branches and leaves and explain why trees are useful and interpretable.
objectives: Use a simple decision tree to classify data
Recognize strengths and limitations of tree models

title: K-Nearest Neighbors: Learning from Similar Examples
syllabus: Introduce K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) as an intuitive algorithm that predicts using nearby examples. Explain similarity, distance and the role of K using simple numerical and classification examples.
objectives: Use nearby examples to make predictions

title: Machine Learning Evaluation Metrics
syllabus: Introduce the idea that an ML model must be evaluated using appropriate metrics. Cover accuracy, precision, recall, F1 score and basic regression metrics such as MAE and RMSE at an intuitive level.
objectives: Understand why evaluation metrics are needed
Choose metrics appropriate to simple problem types

title: Machine Learning Mini Project: From Data to Evaluation
syllabus: Combine the first Machine Learning concepts into a complete small project: define a problem, identify features and target, prepare a dataset, choose a basic model, train it, make predictions and evaluate results.

title: Loss Functions: Measuring Model Error
syllabus: Introduce loss functions as mathematical ways of measuring how far a model's prediction is from the desired answer. Explain why different ML problems use different loss functions and connect loss to model learning.
objectives: Understand the purpose of a loss function
Understand the difference between prediction and target
Understand why minimizing loss helps training

title: Gradient Descent: How Models Improve
syllabus: Introduce gradient descent as an optimization method used to adjust model parameters in a direction that reduces loss. Explain the concept intuitively using a hill-and-valley analogy before introducing the mathematical idea.
objectives: Understand the relationship between parameters and loss
Understand why repeated updates improve a model
Prepare for deeper neural-network training concepts

title: Learning Rate and Training Steps
syllabus: Explain learning rate as a key training parameter controlling how large model updates are. Show the problems of updates that are too large or too small and introduce the idea of training steps and convergence.
objectives: Recognize problems caused by inappropriate learning rates
Understand the relationship between learning rate and training speed

title: Overfitting and Underfitting
syllabus: Explain why an ML model may learn training data too closely or fail to learn enough useful patterns. Introduce overfitting, underfitting and the goal of good generalization using intuitive examples.
objectives: Identify signs of poor model fitting

title: Regularization: Controlling Overfitting
syllabus: Introduce regularization as a family of techniques that discourage overly complex models and help improve generalization. Explain the intuition behind L1 and L2 regularization without requiring advanced mathematics.
objectives: Understand why model complexity can be harmful
Understand the basic idea of L1 regularization
Understand the basic idea of L2 regularization

title: Feature Scaling and Normalization
syllabus: Explain why numerical features with very different scales can affect some ML algorithms. Introduce normalization and standardization conceptually and show when feature scaling is important.
objectives: Recognize algorithms sensitive to feature scale
Prepare data appropriately for simple ML workflows

title: Categorical Data and Feature Encoding
syllabus: Explain how Machine Learning systems handle categorical information such as city, product type or department. Introduce encoding methods such as one-hot encoding and explain why raw text categories cannot always be used directly as numerical inputs.
objectives: Recognize potential problems with inappropriate encoding

title: Cross-Validation: Testing Models More Reliably
syllabus: Introduce cross-validation as a method for evaluating models across multiple train-validation splits. Explain the intuition behind k-fold cross-validation and why it can provide a more stable estimate of model performance.
objectives: Recognize why a single split can be misleading
Use cross-validation conceptually for model comparison

title: Comparing Machine Learning Models
syllabus: Teach a systematic approach to comparing different ML algorithms using the same problem, data splits and evaluation metrics. Cover accuracy, generalization, speed, interpretability and resource requirements.
objectives: Select a model based on practical requirements

title: Machine Learning Model Comparison Project
syllabus: Complete a structured ML experiment in which multiple models solve the same problem. Compare preprocessing, training, validation, evaluation metrics, errors, generalization and practical trade-offs, then justify the final model choice.
objectives: Choose and justify the final model

title: What Is a Neural Network?
syllabus: Begin the Deep Learning section by building a deeper understanding of neural networks. Explain artificial neurons, inputs, weights, bias and outputs using intuitive examples before introducing mathematical notation.

title: Activation Functions: Giving Neural Networks Nonlinearity
syllabus: Explain why neural networks need activation functions and introduce common functions such as ReLU, sigmoid and tanh. Focus on their role and intuition before advanced mathematics.
objectives: Recognize that different architectures may use different activations

title: Neural Network Layers
syllabus: Explain input, hidden and output layers and how multiple layers transform information. Introduce shallow and deep networks and explain how learned representations become increasingly useful for complex tasks.

title: Forward Propagation: From Input to Prediction
syllabus: Teach the forward pass through a neural network: inputs are combined with weights and bias, activation functions transform values and information moves through layers to produce an output.

title: Backpropagation: How Neural Networks Learn
syllabus: Introduce backpropagation as the process used to calculate how model parameters contributed to prediction error so that optimization can update them. Explain the concept intuitively without requiring learners to memorize complex calculus.
objectives: Connect prediction error to parameter updates
Understand how backpropagation works with gradient descent

title: Epochs, Batches and Iterations
syllabus: Explain how training data is processed in batches and repeated across epochs. Introduce batch size, iteration and training duration and show how these concepts affect neural-network training.
objectives: Understand how datasets are repeatedly processed during training

title: Optimizers for Neural Network Training
syllabus: Introduce optimization algorithms used to update neural-network parameters. Explain basic gradient descent and introduce SGD, Momentum, RMSProp and Adam at a conceptual level.
objectives: Recognize Adam and other modern optimizers

title: Training a Neural Network: The Complete Learning Loop
syllabus: Combine forward propagation, loss calculation, backpropagation and optimization into the complete neural-network training loop. Explain how the cycle repeats across batches and epochs.
objectives: Understand the complete neural-network training loop

title: Neural Network Training Problems
syllabus: Introduce common problems in neural-network training including overfitting, underfitting, vanishing gradients, exploding gradients and unstable training. Explain the basic techniques used to address them.
objectives: Understand the purpose of techniques such as normalization, suitable initialization and regularization

title: First Deep Learning Project
syllabus: Complete a beginner-friendly Deep Learning project from dataset preparation through neural-network design, training, validation and evaluation. The goal is to connect the concepts from Days 91–99 into one complete mental and practical workflow.

title: How AI Represents Images
syllabus: Introduce images as numerical data. Explain pixels, image dimensions, color channels and tensors, showing how a computer converts visual information into numerical representations that neural networks can process.
objectives: Understand how images become numerical input for AI

title: What Is Convolution?
syllabus: Introduce convolution as the fundamental operation behind Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). Explain how a small filter moves across an image to detect local patterns such as edges and textures.
objectives: Understand how filters move across images

title: Feature Maps and Learned Visual Features
syllabus: Explain how convolution produces feature maps and how different CNN layers can learn increasingly complex visual patterns, from edges and textures to shapes and object parts.
objectives: Understand early and deeper CNN layers
Connect feature extraction with image recognition

title: Pooling and Spatial Reduction
syllabus: Introduce pooling operations such as max pooling and explain how they reduce spatial dimensions while preserving useful information. Discuss the benefits and limitations of spatial downsampling.
objectives: Understand why pooling can reduce computation

title: Building a Convolutional Neural Network
syllabus: Combine convolution, activation functions, pooling and final prediction layers into a complete CNN architecture. Explain the flow from raw image input to classification output.
objectives: Trace an image through a CNN

title: Image Classification with CNNs
syllabus: Teach image classification using CNNs. Explain how a model learns to assign images to categories and introduce training data, validation data, prediction probabilities and classification metrics.
objectives: Train the concept of image categories
Recognize common sources of classification errors

title: Data Augmentation for Computer Vision
syllabus: Explain data augmentation as a way of creating varied training examples through transformations such as cropping, flipping, rotation and brightness changes. Explain how augmentation can improve generalization when used appropriately.
objectives: Understand why augmentation can reduce overfitting

title: Transfer Learning for Computer Vision
syllabus: Introduce transfer learning: using knowledge learned by a pretrained vision model as a starting point for a new task. Explain feature reuse, fine-tuning and why transfer learning can reduce data and training requirements.
objectives: Recognize when transfer learning is useful

title: CNN Errors and Visual Model Evaluation
syllabus: Teach how to inspect computer-vision model failures using confusion matrices, incorrect predictions, class imbalance and visual error analysis. Explain why accuracy alone may not reveal important weaknesses.

title: Computer Vision CNN Project
syllabus: Complete an end-to-end CNN project covering image data preparation, augmentation, model architecture, training, validation, evaluation, transfer learning and error analysis.
objectives: Train and validate an image model
Use augmentation or transfer learning appropriately

title: What Is Object Detection?
syllabus: Introduce object detection as the task of finding and identifying multiple objects within an image. Explain the difference between image classification and object detection using bounding boxes and object labels.
objectives: Understand detection labels and confidence scores

title: Bounding Boxes and Intersection over Union
syllabus: Explain how object locations are represented with bounding boxes and introduce Intersection over Union (IoU) as a way to measure the overlap between predicted and ground-truth boxes.
objectives: Understand why overlap quality matters in object detection

title: Object Detection Metrics: Precision, Recall and mAP
syllabus: Introduce evaluation methods for object detection, including precision, recall, confidence thresholds and mean Average Precision (mAP). Explain why detection evaluation considers both object identity and location.
objectives: Understand mAP at a high level

title: How Modern Object Detection Models Work
syllabus: Introduce the major ideas behind modern object detectors without tying the curriculum to one specific software library or model version. Explain single-stage and two-stage detection approaches and the basic detection pipeline.
objectives: Understand object detector architecture at a high level

title: Non-Maximum Suppression
syllabus: Explain why an object detector may produce multiple overlapping predictions for the same object and introduce Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS) as a method for retaining strong detections while removing redundant ones.
objectives: Recognize why post-processing is needed in object detection

title: Image Segmentation: Understanding Pixels
syllabus: Introduce image segmentation as assigning information at the pixel level. Explain how segmentation differs from classification and object detection and why pixel-level understanding is useful.

title: Semantic Segmentation vs Instance Segmentation
syllabus: Explain the difference between semantic segmentation, which assigns classes to pixels, and instance segmentation, which distinguishes individual objects of the same class.
objectives: Compare pixel-level class labeling and object-level separation
Understand the concept of segmentation masks

title: Vision Transformers: Beyond CNNs
syllabus: Introduce Vision Transformers (ViTs) as an alternative architecture for visual learning. Explain image patches, embeddings and attention at an intuitive level and compare the broad ideas behind CNNs and Vision Transformers.
objectives: Understand the basic role of attention
Compare CNNs and Vision Transformers conceptually

title: Visual Embeddings and Image Search
syllabus: Explain how images can be represented as numerical embeddings that capture useful visual information. Introduce similarity search and image retrieval, including the basic idea of comparing embeddings.
objectives: Connect embeddings with modern AI search systems

title: Advanced Computer Vision Project
syllabus: Complete an advanced computer-vision workflow that combines detection or segmentation with model evaluation and visual analysis. Introduce practical design decisions involving accuracy, speed, data quality and deployment constraints.

title: How AI Represents Human Language
syllabus: Begin the Natural Language Processing section by explaining how computers convert human language into representations that AI models can process. Introduce text, characters, words, tokens and numerical representations.
objectives: Understand why computers need numerical representations

title: Tokenization: Breaking Text into Tokens
syllabus: Explain tokenization as the process of converting text into smaller units that a language model can process. Explain that tokens may represent words, parts of words, characters or other units depending on the tokenizer.
objectives: Recognize that token count is not the same as word count

title: Text Embeddings: Turning Meaning into Vectors
syllabus: Introduce text embeddings as numerical vector representations that capture useful relationships between pieces of text. Explain semantic similarity and how embeddings support search, recommendation and classification.
objectives: Connect embeddings with modern AI applications

title: Traditional NLP: Classification and Information Extraction
syllabus: Introduce practical NLP tasks such as sentiment classification, topic classification, named entity recognition and information extraction. Explain how language can be converted into structured information.

title: Sequence Models: Why Order Matters
syllabus: Explain why word order and sequence context matter in language. Introduce sequence models and explain how earlier approaches attempted to process language sequentially.

title: RNNs: Recurrent Neural Networks
syllabus: Introduce Recurrent Neural Networks as neural networks designed to process sequences while carrying information from earlier steps. Explain hidden state and the challenges of learning long-range dependencies.

title: LSTMs and GRUs: Better Sequence Memory
syllabus: Explain Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) architectures as improvements designed to handle longer dependencies more effectively than basic RNNs.

title: Attention: Letting Models Focus on Relevant Information
syllabus: Introduce the attention mechanism as a way for a model to assign different importance to different parts of an input when processing a task. Use intuitive language examples before introducing queries, keys and values.
objectives: Understand why attention helps long-range relationships
Introduce queries, keys and values conceptually

title: Self-Attention: Understanding Relationships Within Text
syllabus: Explain self-attention, where tokens attend to other tokens within the same sequence. Introduce the conceptual flow from queries, keys and values to attention weights and contextual representations.
objectives: Understand queries, keys and values more deeply

title: Why Transformers Changed AI
syllabus: Explain the Transformer architecture at a high level and why it became foundational to modern language and multimodal AI. Cover attention-based processing, parallelization, encoder-decoder ideas and the path toward Large Language Models.

title: Inside a Transformer: The Complete Architecture
syllabus: Build a complete mental model of the Transformer architecture by connecting token embeddings, positional information, self-attention, feed-forward networks, normalization, residual connections and stacked layers.
objectives: Trace information through a Transformer layer

title: Positional Information: Understanding Word Order
syllabus: Explain why a Transformer needs information about token positions because self-attention alone does not inherently provide ordinary sequence order. Introduce positional representations and modern positional approaches conceptually.
objectives: Understand why position affects language meaning
Recognize that Transformers can use different positional methods

title: Encoder, Decoder and Encoder-Decoder Transformers
syllabus: Explain the three major Transformer design patterns: encoder-only, decoder-only and encoder-decoder models. Show how their architectures suit tasks such as understanding, generation and sequence transformation.
objectives: Connect architecture choices with AI tasks

title: Next-Token Prediction: The Core Idea Behind Language Models
syllabus: Explain how autoregressive language models learn to predict the next token from previous context. Show how a seemingly simple training objective can produce powerful language-generation capabilities at scale.
objectives: Connect next-token prediction with text generation

title: Pretraining Large Language Models
syllabus: Explain the pretraining stage of an LLM: large-scale data, tokenization, prediction objectives, optimization and repeated training. Discuss the difference between learning general language patterns and learning a specific application.
objectives: Understand training data at a high level

title: Scaling Laws and Why Bigger Models Can Learn More
syllabus: Introduce the idea of scaling relationships between model size, data, computation and performance. Explain why scaling can improve capabilities while also introducing cost, infrastructure and evaluation challenges.
objectives: Understand the relationship between data and computation
Recognize that scale alone does not guarantee useful behavior

title: Parameters, Weights and Model Memory
syllabus: Explain parameters and weights as learned numerical values inside neural networks. Clarify what parameter count does and does not mean and explain the relationship between parameters, model capacity and memory requirements.
objectives: Understand why parameter count affects memory
Avoid common misconceptions about parameter counts

title: LLM Inference: How a Trained Model Generates Text
syllabus: Explain inference as the process of using a trained model to produce predictions. Teach token-by-token generation, context, probability distributions and the distinction between training and inference.

title: Sampling, Temperature and Generation Controls
syllabus: Explain how an LLM chooses the next token and introduce generation controls such as temperature, top-k and top-p conceptually. Explain the trade-off between deterministic and varied outputs.

title: LLM Capabilities, Limitations and Evaluation
syllabus: Develop a realistic understanding of what Large Language Models can and cannot reliably do. Cover reasoning-like behavior, summarization, translation, coding, knowledge limitations, hallucinations, context limitations and the importance of evaluation.
objectives: Understand why LLM outputs require evaluation
Develop responsible expectations of language models

title: What Is Generative AI?
syllabus: Introduce Generative AI as AI that can create new content such as text, images, audio, video and code. Distinguish generation from prediction, classification and traditional automation.
objectives: Identify major types of generated content
Understand the relationship between Generative AI and foundation models

title: Text Generation with Language Models
syllabus: Explain how language models generate text from prompts by repeatedly predicting tokens. Introduce completion, instruction following, structured generation and common text-generation applications.

title: Image Generation with AI
syllabus: Explain how Generative AI can create images from text and other inputs. Introduce text-to-image generation, image-to-image transformation, conditioning and the role of learned visual representations.

title: Diffusion Models: The Core Idea
syllabus: Introduce diffusion models using the intuitive idea of gradually adding noise and learning to reverse the process to create meaningful data. Explain the high-level training and generation process without requiring advanced mathematics.

title: Latent Space and Latent Diffusion
syllabus: Explain latent representations as compact spaces where meaningful information can be represented. Introduce latent diffusion conceptually and explain why generating in a latent space can improve efficiency.
objectives: Understand why latent representations are useful

title: AI Audio Generation: Speech, Music and Sound
syllabus: Introduce generative AI for audio, including text-to-speech, speech synthesis, voice transformation, music generation and sound generation. Explain the difference between speech understanding and speech generation.
objectives: Distinguish speech recognition from speech generation

title: AI Video Generation
syllabus: Explain video generation as a multimodal generative problem involving visual content, time, motion and sometimes audio. Introduce text-to-video, image-to-video and video transformation at a conceptual level.

title: Multimodal Generative AI
syllabus: Explain models and systems that can understand or generate multiple modalities such as text, images, audio and video. Teach how multimodal inputs can be combined to solve tasks that a single modality cannot handle well.

title: Controlling Generative AI Output
syllabus: Teach practical methods for controlling generated content through prompts, conditioning, parameters, constraints, references and structured output requirements. Explain why generation remains probabilistic.
objectives: Improve consistency and usefulness of generated content

title: Generative AI Project: Create a Multimodal Content Workflow
syllabus: Design a practical Generative AI workflow that combines one or more modalities to create useful content. Require learners to define the goal, select suitable AI capabilities, design inputs, evaluate outputs and document limitations and responsible-use considerations.

title: Advanced Prompt Engineering: The Anatomy of a Reliable Prompt
syllabus: Move from basic prompting to systematic prompt engineering. Teach the major components of a reliable prompt: objective, context, inputs, constraints, output requirements, examples and evaluation criteria.

title: Role, Context and Task Instructions
syllabus: Teach how to clearly communicate the AI system's intended role, relevant context and exact task. Explain why unnecessary role-playing should not replace precise task instructions.

title: Constraints and Output Specifications
syllabus: Explain how constraints such as length, language, audience, format, allowed content and required fields can make AI outputs more predictable and useful.

title: Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Prompting
syllabus: Explain zero-shot prompting and few-shot prompting and show how examples can teach a model the desired pattern without changing its underlying parameters.

title: Prompt Decomposition: Breaking Complex Tasks into Steps
syllabus: Teach learners to divide complex tasks into smaller logical stages rather than asking for everything in one ambiguous instruction. Introduce task decomposition, intermediate artifacts and multi-step workflows.

title: Reasoning-Oriented Prompt Design
syllabus: Explain how prompts can encourage careful problem solving, verification and structured analysis without treating hidden chain-of-thought as a required output. Teach concise reasoning summaries, checks, assumptions and final-answer validation.
objectives: Separate analysis requirements from final output
Design prompts for complex tasks responsibly

title: Structured Output: JSON, Tables and Schemas
syllabus: Teach how to request machine-readable outputs using JSON, tables, lists and explicit schemas. Explain field definitions, required values, data types and validation.
objectives: Prepare AI output for software systems

title: Prompt Testing and Evaluation
syllabus: Introduce prompt evaluation as an engineering process rather than judging one response. Teach test cases, expected behavior, edge cases, consistency, factuality and task-specific quality criteria.

title: Prompt Optimization and Version Control
syllabus: Teach prompt iteration as an engineering cycle: baseline, test, measure, modify, compare and document. Introduce prompt versioning and change tracking for reliable applications.

title: Production Prompt System Project
syllabus: Design a reusable production-style prompt system for a practical application. The project should include clear instructions, input handling, structured output, test cases, evaluation criteria, versioning and failure handling.

title: Why Large Language Models Need External Knowledge
syllabus: Explain why an LLM's internal learned knowledge is not the same as access to current, private or organization-specific information. Introduce the need for external knowledge systems and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
objectives: Understand the knowledge limitations of LLMs
Distinguish model knowledge from external information
Understand why retrieval can improve answers

title: Documents as AI Knowledge Sources
syllabus: Teach how documents such as PDFs, web pages, manuals, policies, books and company records can become knowledge sources for AI applications. Explain document ingestion and the difference between storing files and making their content searchable.
objectives: Understand why raw file storage is not enough for intelligent retrieval

title: Document Chunking for Retrieval
syllabus: Explain why large documents are usually divided into smaller chunks before retrieval. Teach chunk size, overlap, semantic boundaries and metadata while explaining the trade-off between too-small and too-large chunks.

title: Embeddings for Semantic Search
syllabus: Explain how embedding models convert text into vectors that capture useful semantic relationships. Show how semantically similar questions and documents can be matched even when they do not use exactly the same words.
objectives: Connect questions with relevant document chunks
Understand why keyword matching alone can be insufficient

title: Vector Databases and Vector Stores
syllabus: Introduce vector databases and vector stores as systems designed to store embeddings and retrieve similar items efficiently. Explain vectors, metadata, indexing and similarity search at a practical level.

title: Similarity Search and Retrieval
syllabus: Explain how a user's question is converted into a representation and used to retrieve relevant information. Introduce similarity measures conceptually and explain top-k retrieval and relevance ranking.

title: The RAG Pipeline: Retrieve Before Generating
syllabus: Connect ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector storage, retrieval and generation into one complete Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline.

title: Grounded Answers and Citations
syllabus: Teach how RAG applications can ground answers in retrieved sources. Explain source attribution, citations, evidence snippets and the importance of distinguishing retrieved evidence from model-generated interpretation.

title: RAG Quality: Retrieval and Answer Evaluation
syllabus: Explain that a RAG system can fail because retrieval is poor or because the LLM misuses good retrieved information. Introduce retrieval quality, relevance, completeness, faithfulness and answer quality as separate evaluation dimensions.
objectives: Separate retrieval errors from generation errors

title: Build a Complete RAG Knowledge Assistant
syllabus: Design an end-to-end RAG application using a practical knowledge collection. The project should cover document ingestion, chunking, embeddings, vector search, retrieval, prompt construction, grounded generation, citations and evaluation.

title: Prompting vs Fine-Tuning: Choosing the Right Approach
syllabus: Explain the difference between changing an AI system through prompts and changing model parameters through fine-tuning. Teach when prompting, RAG, fine-tuning or a combination of approaches is appropriate.
objectives: Identify problems that do not require fine-tuning

title: What Is Fine-Tuning?
syllabus: Introduce fine-tuning as additional training of a pretrained model on task-specific data. Explain how the model's learned parameters can be adapted to produce desired behavior for a narrower task.
objectives: Distinguish fine-tuning from training a model from scratch

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning and Instruction Tuning
syllabus: Explain supervised fine-tuning using examples of inputs and desired outputs. Introduce instruction tuning and explain how curated instruction-response datasets can improve a model's ability to follow tasks.
objectives: Recognize the importance of high-quality examples

title: Creating a Fine-Tuning Dataset
syllabus: Teach how to design a useful fine-tuning dataset, including task definition, input formatting, expected outputs, consistency, diversity, edge cases and metadata.

title: Data Quality, Bias and Dataset Contamination
syllabus: Explain why fine-tuning quality depends heavily on training data quality. Cover incorrect labels, duplicated examples, contradictory instructions, bias, sensitive information and possible contamination or leakage.
objectives: Understand data leakage and contamination risks

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
syllabus: Introduce Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) as a family of techniques that adapt models while updating a much smaller number of parameters than full fine-tuning.
objectives: Understand why full fine-tuning can be expensive
Understand the idea of updating fewer parameters
Compare full fine-tuning and parameter-efficient approaches

title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation
syllabus: Introduce Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) as a widely used parameter-efficient adaptation method. Explain the core intuition of learning small low-rank updates instead of modifying all original model weights.
objectives: Understand why LoRA reduces trainable parameters
Understand the relationship between base models and adapters

title: Fine-Tuning Evaluation and Model Comparison
syllabus: Teach how to determine whether fine-tuning actually improved a model. Introduce held-out evaluation data, task-specific metrics, baseline comparison, qualitative testing and regression testing.

title: Fine-Tuning Risks and Operational Costs
syllabus: Explain practical risks of fine-tuning, including overfitting, loss of general capabilities, biased behavior, poor data quality, training cost, model storage and ongoing maintenance.

title: Fine-Tuning Project: Adapt a Model for a Specific Task
syllabus: Design a complete model-adaptation project. Define a task, create and validate a dataset, establish a baseline, select an adaptation method, fine-tune or simulate the workflow, evaluate results and document whether fine-tuning was justified.
objectives: Decide whether adaptation improved the application

title: What Is an AI Agent?
syllabus: Introduce AI agents as systems that use AI models together with instructions, tools, state and feedback to accomplish goals. Clearly distinguish an agent from a simple chatbot or single prompt.
objectives: Understand the difference between chatbots and agents

title: LLM + Tools: Giving AI the Ability to Act
syllabus: Explain how an LLM can be connected to external tools such as calculators, databases, search systems, APIs and application functions. Emphasize that the model does not automatically gain access to tools; the surrounding software controls access.
objectives: Understand the role of application code
Distinguish model reasoning from tool execution

title: Function Calling and Tool Calling
syllabus: Introduce function calling and tool calling as structured ways for an AI model to request an application function. Explain function names, arguments, schemas, validation and returning tool results to the model.

title: APIs: Connecting AI to the Real World
syllabus: Explain APIs as controlled interfaces through which software systems exchange data and actions. Teach how an AI application can use APIs for weather, search, payments, databases, messaging and other services while respecting permissions.
objectives: Connect AI systems with external services safely

title: Tool Selection: Choosing the Right Action
syllabus: Teach how an agent decides which available tool is appropriate for a task. Explain tool descriptions, schemas, constraints, ambiguity and the importance of validating tool selection before execution.

title: Planning and Task Decomposition in AI Agents
syllabus: Explain how complex goals can be divided into smaller actions. Introduce planning patterns, dependencies, intermediate results and verification while emphasizing that agent plans should remain bounded and observable.

title: Memory and State in AI Agents
syllabus: Explain the difference between conversation context, short-term state and persistent memory. Teach why an agent needs carefully designed state management and why not every piece of information should be permanently remembered.

title: The Agent Loop: Observe, Decide, Act and Verify
syllabus: Introduce the basic agent loop in which the system receives a goal, observes available information, decides on an action, executes a tool, observes the result and continues or finishes. Explain stopping conditions and loop limits.

title: Agent Safety, Permissions and Human Approval
syllabus: Teach why agents that can take actions require stronger controls than systems that only generate text. Cover least-privilege access, confirmation for high-impact actions, tool restrictions, logging and human-in-the-loop approval.

title: Build a Practical AI Agent
syllabus: Design an end-to-end AI agent that receives a goal, selects approved tools, executes bounded actions, maintains necessary state, verifies results and produces a final response. Include logging, failure handling and human approval for sensitive actions.

title: What Is AI Automation?
syllabus: Introduce AI automation as the combination of AI capabilities with software workflows that can automatically process information and perform defined actions. Explain the difference between ordinary automation, AI-assisted automation and autonomous agents.
objectives: Compare traditional automation and AI automation

title: Deterministic Workflows vs AI Workflows
syllabus: Explain deterministic workflows where predefined rules produce predictable results and AI workflows where models interpret or generate information. Teach how to combine both approaches instead of unnecessarily using AI for deterministic tasks.

title: Triggers: Starting an Automated AI Workflow
syllabus: Teach triggers as events that start workflows. Cover user actions, new files, incoming messages, database events, schedules and external events. Explain the importance of validating trigger data.

title: Actions, Conditions and Workflow Branches
syllabus: Explain how workflows perform actions and make rule-based branches. Teach conditions, filters, approvals and different paths depending on input or AI classification.
objectives: Combine AI decisions with deterministic rules

title: APIs and Webhooks in AI Automation
syllabus: Teach how APIs and webhooks allow automated systems to communicate with external services. Explain request and response flow, authentication, event delivery and basic reliability considerations.

title: Workflow Orchestration and Multi-Step AI Pipelines
syllabus: Explain orchestration as coordinating multiple workflow steps, services and AI calls. Teach sequential steps, parallel work, dependencies, intermediate data and controlled retries.

title: Errors, Retries and Failure Handling
syllabus: Teach that production automation must expect failures such as API errors, timeouts, invalid AI outputs, missing data and service outages. Introduce validation, retries, fallback paths, dead-letter handling and alerts.

title: Scheduling, Queues and Background AI Jobs
syllabus: Introduce scheduled automation, background jobs and queues for workloads that should not block a user's request. Explain job status, concurrency, rate limits and retry strategies.

title: Monitoring, Logging and Cost Control
syllabus: Explain how production AI automation needs observability. Teach workflow logs, execution status, AI latency, token usage, API costs, failures and basic performance monitoring.

title: AI Automation Project: Build a Production Workflow
syllabus: Design a complete AI automation system from trigger to final action. Include input validation, AI processing, deterministic rules, API or webhook integration, retries, logging, monitoring, cost controls and human approval where required.

title: AI Application Engineering: From Model to Product
syllabus: Introduce AI application engineering as the discipline of turning AI models into reliable user-facing products. Explain the major layers of an AI application: user interface, application logic, AI model, data, tools and infrastructure.
objectives: Identify the major components of an AI product
Understand the difference between an AI model and an AI application
Understand the flow from user input to AI output

title: AI Model APIs: Connecting Applications to AI
syllabus: Explain how applications communicate with hosted AI models through APIs. Cover requests, model selection, messages or inputs, parameters, responses and basic error handling.

title: SDKs and AI Development Libraries
syllabus: Introduce Software Development Kits (SDKs) and AI libraries that simplify communication with model providers and AI infrastructure. Explain the difference between using a raw API and an SDK.
objectives: Choose tools based on project requirements

title: Context Management in AI Applications
syllabus: Explain how AI applications manage conversation history, user information, retrieved documents, instructions and tool results within the model's available context. Teach context selection, summarization and prioritization.

title: Structured AI Outputs for Software Systems
syllabus: Teach how AI applications can request structured results that software can validate and process. Cover schemas, required fields, data types, validation and handling malformed or incomplete outputs.
objectives: Connect AI outputs to application logic

title: Streaming AI Responses and Real-Time UX
syllabus: Explain streaming as delivering generated output progressively instead of waiting for the entire response. Teach why streaming improves perceived responsiveness and what applications must handle during partial output.

title: Multimodal AI APIs
syllabus: Explain how modern AI applications can send and process multiple types of input such as text, images, audio and other supported media. Teach multimodal input design, validation and practical use cases.

title: Authentication, API Keys and Secret Management
syllabus: Teach the security fundamentals of connecting applications to AI services. Explain API keys, environment variables, server-side secrets, access control and why secrets must not be exposed in client-side code.

title: Rate Limits, Caching and AI Cost Optimization
syllabus: Explain why AI applications encounter rate limits, latency and usage costs. Introduce request reduction, caching, batching where appropriate, model selection, token optimization and graceful handling of limits.

title: AI Application Project: Build a Production-Ready AI Feature
syllabus: Design a complete AI-powered application feature connecting a user interface to an AI model API. Include context handling, structured outputs, streaming where appropriate, secure authentication, error handling, rate-limit protection, logging and cost awareness.
objectives: Connect an AI model through an API

title: What Is Responsible AI?
syllabus: Introduce Responsible AI as the practice of designing, developing and using AI systems with attention to safety, fairness, privacy, transparency, accountability, reliability and human well-being.
objectives: Understand why technical performance alone is insufficient

title: AI Hallucinations and Unreliable Outputs
syllabus: Explain AI hallucinations as cases where a model produces information that is unsupported, incorrect or fabricated. Teach why fluent language does not guarantee truth and introduce verification, grounding and uncertainty-aware workflows.
objectives: Understand why language fluency is not proof of accuracy
Understand the role of RAG and external evidence

title: Bias, Fairness and Representation in AI
syllabus: Explain how bias can enter AI systems through data, labels, model design, evaluation and deployment. Introduce fairness as a context-dependent engineering and social concern rather than a single universal metric.
objectives: Recognize the need for context-specific evaluation

title: Privacy and Personal Data in AI Systems
syllabus: Teach why AI applications must carefully handle personal and confidential information. Cover data minimization, access control, retention, secure processing and the risks of sending sensitive information to external AI services.

title: Data Security and AI Application Security
syllabus: Introduce security principles for AI applications, including secure APIs, authentication, authorization, encryption, secret management, input validation and protection of model-connected systems.

title: Prompt Injection and Indirect Prompt Injection
syllabus: Explain prompt injection as an attack where untrusted instructions attempt to manipulate an AI system into ignoring intended behavior or performing unauthorized actions. Introduce indirect prompt injection through external content and teach layered defenses.
objectives: Distinguish trusted instructions from untrusted data
Design basic defenses and validation layers

title: Adversarial Attacks and AI Robustness
syllabus: Introduce adversarial attacks as inputs or manipulations designed to cause unwanted model behavior. Explain robustness, adversarial examples, data poisoning and model abuse at a conceptual level.

title: Human-in-the-Loop AI
syllabus: Explain when AI decisions should be reviewed, approved or corrected by humans. Teach escalation, confidence thresholds, high-impact decisions, approval workflows and the principle that automation level should match risk.

title: AI Transparency, Explainability and Accountability
syllabus: Explain why users and organizations may need to understand how an AI system is being used, what information influenced an output, what limitations exist and who is responsible for decisions. Introduce explainability, documentation and auditability.

title: Responsible AI Project: Design a Safe AI System
syllabus: Design a practical AI system with explicit risk analysis, privacy controls, security boundaries, hallucination mitigation, bias considerations, human oversight, monitoring and incident-response procedures.
objectives: Create a responsible AI deployment plan

title: Why AI Systems Need Continuous Evaluation
syllabus: Introduce AI evaluation as a continuous engineering process. Explain why an AI system can change behavior because of model updates, prompt changes, data changes, tool changes and changing user inputs.
objectives: Understand why one successful response is insufficient
Identify sources of AI behavior changes
Recognize the need for continuous testing

title: Building an AI Evaluation Dataset
syllabus: Teach how to create a representative evaluation dataset containing normal cases, difficult cases, edge cases and failure cases. Explain the difference between training data, validation data and evaluation data.
objectives: Separate evaluation data from training data

title: Accuracy, Precision, Recall and F1
syllabus: Teach foundational classification metrics and explain when accuracy can be misleading. Introduce precision, recall and F1 score using simple real-world examples before connecting them to AI evaluation.
objectives: Choose appropriate metrics for classification tasks

title: Evaluating Generative AI Outputs
syllabus: Explain why generated text cannot always be evaluated using simple exact-match metrics. Introduce relevance, completeness, clarity, factuality, instruction following and task-specific quality criteria.

title: Factuality, Grounding and Faithfulness
syllabus: Teach the difference between a response being relevant and being factually supported. Explain grounding and faithfulness, especially for RAG systems, and show how evidence can be used to evaluate generated claims.

title: Evaluating AI Safety and Security
syllabus: Introduce safety evaluation using harmful, manipulative, privacy-sensitive and adversarial test cases. Teach how to test refusal behavior, data protection, tool restrictions and prompt-injection resistance.

title: Human Evaluation and Expert Review
syllabus: Explain when human reviewers are necessary for evaluating AI quality. Teach evaluation rubrics, blind comparison, reviewer consistency, domain expertise and separating factual correctness from personal preference.

title: Automated Evaluation and AI-as-a-Judge
syllabus: Introduce automated evaluation methods, including rule-based checks and model-based judging. Explain the benefits and limitations of using one AI model to evaluate another AI output and why calibration against human judgments matters.
objectives: Compare automated evaluation with human evaluation

title: Regression Testing and AI Quality Gates
syllabus: Teach how to prevent changes from silently degrading an AI system. Introduce regression test suites, pass thresholds, quality gates and comparing new model or prompt versions against an established baseline.

title: AI Evaluation Project: Build a Quality System
syllabus: Design an end-to-end evaluation framework for an AI application. Include representative test data, task metrics, generative-output evaluation, factuality checks, safety tests, human review, automated evaluation, regression testing and deployment quality gates.

title: Data Is the Foundation of AI
syllabus: Explain why AI systems depend on data for training, retrieval, evaluation and decision-making. Distinguish training data, evaluation data, operational data and knowledge-base data.
objectives: Understand the role of data in AI
Identify major types of AI data
Connect data quality with AI quality

title: AI Data Collection and Data Sources
syllabus: Teach how AI projects obtain data from databases, APIs, documents, sensors, user interactions, public sources and organizational systems. Explain source reliability, permissions, provenance and legal or policy considerations.

title: Data Cleaning and Normalization
syllabus: Explain how raw data can contain missing values, duplicates, inconsistent formats, invalid records and noise. Teach basic cleaning, normalization and validation concepts before data enters an AI pipeline.

title: Data Labeling and Annotation
syllabus: Introduce labeling and annotation for supervised machine learning and AI evaluation. Explain classification labels, bounding boxes, segmentation, text annotations and quality-control processes.

title: Metadata: Making AI Data Understandable
syllabus: Teach metadata as information that describes data, such as source, date, author, category, language, permissions, version and document type. Explain why metadata is critical for filtering, retrieval, governance and auditing.

title: Data Pipelines for AI
syllabus: Introduce an AI data pipeline as a repeatable flow from data ingestion through cleaning, transformation, storage and delivery to AI systems. Explain batch and streaming pipelines conceptually.
objectives: Compare batch and streaming data flows

title: Data Quality Testing for AI
syllabus: Teach systematic data-quality checks such as completeness, uniqueness, validity, consistency, accuracy, freshness and distribution monitoring. Explain why data tests should run automatically in production pipelines.

title: Synthetic Data for AI
syllabus: Explain synthetic data as artificially generated data designed to supplement or simulate real-world data. Teach useful applications, quality checks, diversity, privacy considerations and the risk of reinforcing errors or bias.

title: Data Versioning, Lineage and Reproducibility
syllabus: Teach how AI teams track which data produced a particular model, evaluation result or knowledge base. Introduce data versions, lineage, reproducibility and change tracking.
objectives: Connect data versions with model versions

title: AI Data Engineering Project: Build a Knowledge Pipeline
syllabus: Design a production-style AI data pipeline that collects source data, validates permissions, cleans and normalizes content, adds metadata, creates versions, performs quality checks and delivers trusted data to an AI or RAG application.
objectives: Deliver reliable data to an AI system

title: What Is MLOps and AI Operations?
